Choosing how the model reads

Source: vignettes/readers.Rmd
readers.Rmd

Once a document is cut into chunks, a reading strategy decides how the model works through them. It can send everything in one request, ask each chunk separately and combine the answers, or pick the few chunks most like the question and ignore the rest. harnessr calls these strategies readers. The reader sets most of a run’s cost and much of its answer’s quality: the same chunks read two ways can take one request or dozens, and can find a fact or miss it.

This guide explains each reader, runs them all on one document, and gives you a way to choose. vignette("harnessr") introduces the package and its ideas.

Setting up

The examples run for free because a stand-in plays the model. It answers each kind of request as a model would: it scores an excerpt when a reader asks for a score and quotes when a reader asks for a quotation, so every reader does its normal work. You can skip its details.

library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

stand_in <- function(messages, params) {
  instructions <- messages[[1]]$content
  everything <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) m$content, character(1)),
                      collapse = "\n")
  task <- if (is.null(params$schema_name)) "" else params$schema_name
  if (task == "relevance") {        # rerank: score one excerpt from 0 to 10
    excerpt <- messages[[length(messages)]]$content
    if (grepl("revenue", excerpt, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      return('{"score": 9, "reason": "States revenue."}')
    }
    return('{"score": 2, "reason": "About something else."}')
  }
  if (task == "iterative_step") {   # iterative: can I answer yet?
    return('{"can_answer": true, "answer": "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", "next_query": ""}')
  }
  if (task == "reading_plan") {     # preview: which sections to read
    return('{"sections": [{"id": 1, "treatment": "read", "reason": "States revenue."}]}')
  }
  if (grepl("You extract evidence", instructions, fixed = TRUE)) {   # skim: quote
    quote <- regmatches(everything,
                        regexpr("[^.\n]*revenue of [0-9.]+ million dollars[^.\n]*", everything))
    return(if (length(quote)) quote else "NONE")
  }
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars."
}

With embedder = "lexical", the readers that search for similar text use word matching computed on your machine instead of a paid embedding service. “Embeddings” below covers the difference.

Cut the example report into chunks at its section headings:

chunks <- gr_segment(gr_ingest(gr_example()),
                     list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
gr_chunk_stats(chunks)
#>       method n total_tokens min median mean max over_cap
#> 1 structural 8          557  16   76.5 69.6 102        0

That gives eight chunks. A real report can have hundreds, and the differences below grow with it.

Listing the readers 

gr_readers()[, c("name", "signature", "cost_calls")]
#>            name             signature
#> 1      ensemble   ensemble|sum+1|none
#> 2       extract  all|N+conflicts|none
#> 3  hierarchical     all|N+tree+1|tree
#> 4     iterative topk|rounds*2|forward
#> 5    map_reduce       all|N+logN|tree
#> 6       preview    planned|1+s+1|none
#> 7        refine         all|N|forward
#> 8        rerank         topk|m+1|none
#> 9      retrieve           topk|1|none
#> 10       screen           head|1|none
#> 11         skim          all|N+1|none
#> 12        stuff            all|1|none
#>                                    cost_calls
#> 1                          sum of members + 1
#> 2  N (+1 per conflict with resolve = 'model')
#> 3                       N + fan-in levels + 1
#> 4                        up to 2 x max_rounds
#> 5                                  N + merges
#> 6                    1 + skimmed sections + 1
#> 7                                           N
#> 8                                       m + 1
#> 9                              1 + embeddings
#> 10                                          1
#> 11                                      N + 1
#> 12                                          1

cost_calls gives the number of requests a reader makes as a formula in N, the number of chunks. If the count grows with N, a document a hundred times longer takes a hundred times as many requests.

You pay for tokens, though, and a reader that looks at every chunk sends every token. stuff makes one request at any length, but that request carries the whole document, so its cost grows with the document too. Each request also repeats the instructions and writes its own reply, so among readers that see everything, more requests cost more. The readers that look at a selection of chunks (the topk ones below) cost about the same at any document length.

signature describes how a reader works, in three parts separated by |:

  • which chunks it looks at: all of them; the topk most relevant; the head (opening) of the document; the chunks a planned reading chose; or, for an ensemble, whatever its members looked at;
  • how many requests it makes, the same formula in short;
  • what carries over between requests: none (each request stands alone), tree (answers are combined in stages), or forward (each request builds on the one before).

No two built-in readers share a signature, and ensemble refuses members that do: two readers with one signature are one method under two names.

Every reader on one document

Each general-purpose reader below gets the same question on the same eight chunks. extract and screen are left out because they are built for literature reviews and need a schema or criteria.

read_with <- function(reader) {
  model <- hr_mock_client(stand_in)
  ans <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", model, reader)
  data.frame(reader = reader, requests = length(model$calls()),
             chunks_used = length(ans$chunks_used), partial = ans$partial)
}
readers <- c("stuff", "map_reduce", "refine", "skim", "hierarchical",
             "retrieve", "rerank", "iterative", "preview", "ensemble")
do.call(rbind, lapply(readers, read_with))
#>          reader requests chunks_used partial
#> 1         stuff        1           8   FALSE
#> 2    map_reduce        9           8   FALSE
#> 3        refine        8           8   FALSE
#> 4          skim        9           1   FALSE
#> 5  hierarchical        9           8   FALSE
#> 6      retrieve        1           6   FALSE
#> 7        rerank        9           2   FALSE
#> 8     iterative        1           6   FALSE
#> 9       preview        2           8   FALSE
#> 10     ensemble       11           8   FALSE

Every reader gets the same answer from the stand-in, and no run degraded (partial is FALSE). The work differs: from one request to eleven for eight chunks, and from reading every chunk to relying on one passage. A long document widens the gap. For some readers the number of requests grows with the document and for others it stays fixed, and the cost grows for every reader that reads the whole document.

The readers

stuff: everything in one request

stuff puts the whole document into a single prompt. It is the simplest reader, and usually the cheapest way to have the model read all of a document, with one set of instructions and one reply. Its cost still grows with the document’s length. The model sees everything at once, so it can connect facts from different places.

The context window sets the limit. If the document does not fit, stuff sends what fits, warns, and marks the answer partial (on_overflow = "error" makes it stop instead). Very long prompts also dilute attention, and a model misses details in the middle of a long prompt more easily.

Use it for documents comfortably inside the model’s context window. Recipe: "fast", which answer_document() uses by default for a document of up to 50,000 tokens, or less on a model with a small context window.

map_reduce: every chunk separately, then combined

map_reduce asks the question of each chunk on its own (the “map”), then combines the answers in stages (the “reduce”). It skips nothing, each request is small, and the per-chunk requests can run in parallel. It costs N requests plus the combining steps. It can miss a fact that only makes sense across two chunks, because no single request sees both.

Use it for questions where every mention matters: “list every risk named in this report”. Recipe: "thorough", which answer_document() uses by default for a longer document.

refine: a draft revised chunk by chunk

refine reads the chunks in order and keeps a running answer, revising it with each new chunk. Later text can correct earlier conclusions, which suits documents whose argument develops. It costs N requests that cannot run in parallel, and the running answer can drift.

Use it for narratives and arguments that build. Recipe: "narrative".

skim: quote first, then answer

For each chunk, skim asks the model to copy out any passages that bear on the question, then answers once from those passages alone. The final answer rests on quotations, and harnessr checks them against the text (see “Checking what an answer rests on” below). It costs N + 1 requests, and skim_model can put the per-chunk step on a cheaper model.

Use it for questions where you want the answer tied to exact wording. Recipe: "precise".

hierarchical: summaries of summaries

hierarchical summarises each chunk, then summarises the summaries in groups of fan_in, level by level, until everything fits in one prompt, and answers from that. It suits questions about a whole long document, such as “what is this report’s overall argument?”, and loses detail in the summarising. summary_model can put the summaries on a cheaper model, and max_levels caps the depth.

Use it for long, structured documents where you want an overview. Recipe: "survey".

retrieve: only the most relevant chunks

retrieve turns the question and every chunk into embeddings (lists of numbers that place similar text close together) and sends only the top_k chunks closest to the question, in a single request. The cost of the answer does not grow with the document, so retrieve is the usual choice for finding one fact in something long. The risk is a chunk that answers the question but does not look like it: it can rank below the top_k cut and never reach the model.

Use it for a specific fact in a long document. Recipe: "needle".

rerank: shortlist, then let the model judge

rerank makes a quick word-matching shortlist (rerank_candidates chunks, 20 by default), asks the model to score each from 0 to 10 for relevance, and answers from the chunks scoring at least rerank_min_score. The model judges relevance better than word matching does, at the price of one scoring request per shortlisted chunk. skim_model can do the scoring more cheaply.

If no chunk could be scored, for example because the provider does not support the structured replies the scoring needs, rerank falls back to the word-matching order and warns. If only some chunks were scored, it marks the answer partial.

Use it for long documents where word matching alone picks badly, including scanned ones. Recipe: "scanned".

iterative: look, decide what is missing, look again

iterative retrieves a few chunks and asks the model whether it can answer yet and, if not, what to look for next. Then it retrieves again, up to max_rounds times. It suits questions that need several facts from different places (“how did the drop in margin affect the dividend?”). ans$notes$queries records what it searched for in each round, and ans$notes$stop_reason why it stopped.

Use it for multi-step questions. Recipe: "research".

preview: plan, then read

preview shows the model an outline of the document (section headings, sizes and short excerpts) and asks which sections to read in full, which to skim and which to skip. Then it reads accordingly. It reads every section the plan does not mention, so a plan’s silence cannot lose part of the document. ans$notes$plan records the plan, so you can see that “sections 3 and 5 were not read”. If no usable plan comes back, preview reads everything and marks the answer partial.

Use it for long documents with clear sections, when most of them are irrelevant to the question.

ensemble: several readers, compared

ensemble runs two or more different readers (members, by default retrieve and map_reduce) and asks the model to reconcile their answers. It costs the sum of its members plus one request, and pays off when a wrong answer is expensive. Members must have different signatures: the same method run twice gives no second opinion.

Use it for high-stakes questions. Recipe: "consensus".

extract and screen

extract fills in a table of details (a schema) from every chunk, and screen decides whether a document meets a set of criteria. Both belong to the literature-review workflow in vignette("review").

Choosing a reader

your situation reader recipe cost grows with document length?
the document fits comfortably in one request stuff "fast" yes, though it is one request
one specific fact, long document retrieve "needle" no (embeddings aside)
one fact, and word matching picks badly; scanned pages rerank "scanned" no, fixed by rerank_candidates
every mention must be found map_reduce "thorough" yes
the answer must rest on exact quotations; a short document with every sentence weighed skim "precise" yes
an overview of a long document hierarchical "survey" yes
an argument that develops through the text refine "narrative" yes
several facts combined from different places iterative "research" no, up to max_rounds (embeddings aside)
long document, most sections irrelevant preview none depends on the plan
a wrong answer would be costly ensemble "consensus" as its members

If you are unsure, run two or three readers on a document whose answer you already know and compare them (see “Trying readers on your own documents” below).

Recipes

A recipe names an ingestion, a segmentation and a reader together, with their settings. The table above gives the recipe built on each reader. gr_recipes() returns them all:

do.call(rbind, lapply(names(gr_recipes()), function(n) {
  r <- gr_recipes(n)
  data.frame(recipe = n, segment = r$segment$method, reader = r$read$reader)
}))
#>       recipe    segment       reader
#> 1       fast  paragraph        stuff
#> 2    precise   sentence         skim
#> 3     needle   semantic     retrieve
#> 4   thorough  paragraph   map_reduce
#> 5     survey structural hierarchical
#> 6  narrative  paragraph       refine
#> 7    scanned       page       rerank
#> 8   research structural    iterative
#> 9  consensus  recursive     ensemble
#> 10    legacy  paragraph   map_reduce

answer_document() defaults to "auto", which reads a document of up to 50,000 tokens (less on a model with a small context window) with "fast", in one request, and a longer one with "thorough", one request per chunk. Both send every chunk, and ans$recipe names the one used. gr_read_many(), gr_compare() and the review functions take one fixed recipe and refuse "auto".

Printing a recipe shows every setting on all three steps:

gr_recipes("thorough")
#> <gr_recipe 'thorough'>
#>   ingest  : clean=standard ocr=auto
#>   segment : paragraph (max 1200 tok, overlap 120, min 0)
#>   read    : map_reduce [all|N+logN|tree] model=(the client's)

You can override any of a recipe’s settings by name in the call, as in answer_document(file, question, "needle", top_k = 3). gr_recipe() builds a recipe from scratch, with an example under “Trying readers on your own documents” below.

"legacy" reproduces the previous release’s behaviour (digit stripping, 3000-token paragraph chunks, no overlap), so you can measure the difference instead of assuming it.

Choosing and placing chunks

retrieve, rerank and iterative choose which chunks the model sees. The settings below control that choice and where the chosen chunks go, and each names the readers it applies to.

top_k (retrieve, rerank, iterative) is how many chunks to send, 6 by default. For iterative it is how many each round adds: the chunks gathered in earlier rounds stay in the prompt as long as they fit. With too few, the model can miss the answer; with too many, you pay for text that does not help.

min_score (retrieve) drops chunks less similar to the question than a threshold, though the single best chunk is always kept.

mmr (retrieve, iterative) stops near-duplicates crowding each other out. Plain top-k picks the chunks most like the question, so if three paragraphs say the same thing, all three get in. Below 1, mmr weighs relevance against similarity to the chunks already picked (0.7 is a reasonable start):

repetitive <- paste(c(
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024.",
  "Total revenue reached 45.2 million dollars in the 2024 fiscal year.",
  "In fiscal 2024 the company recorded revenue of 45.2 million dollars.",
  "Headcount grew to 1,204 employees across nine clinical sites.",
  "The board approved a dividend of 0.42 dollars per share in March."),
  collapse = "\n\n")
pieces <- gr_segment(gr_ingest(repetitive), list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 40))
model <- hr_mock_client(stand_in)
picked <- function(mmr) {
  gr_read(pieces, "What was revenue?", model,
          list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 3, mmr = mmr))$chunks_used
}
rbind("top-k (mmr = 1)" = picked(1), "mmr = 0.3" = picked(0.3))
#>                 [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> top-k (mmr = 1)    1    3    2
#> mmr = 0.3          1    4    5

Plain top-k spent all three places on the same fact. mmr = 0.3 kept the best one and used the other two for something different, at no extra cost.

context_order (retrieve, rerank, iterative) decides where the chosen chunks sit in the prompt. Models attend best to the beginning and end of a long prompt, so "edges" puts the best chunk first and the second-best last; "document" keeps the order they appear in the document, which reads more naturally when chunks are consecutive; the default "relevance" puts the best first. context_order moves the chosen chunks and leaves the choice alone.

restate (every reader but extract and screen) repeats the question before the excerpts as well as after them, because a question asked once, after several thousand tokens of text, is a long way from the start of the prompt. "auto" does this when the text is long, "always" and "never" override.

mmr, context_order and restate help on some documents and models and not on others, so test them on yours.

Embeddings

retrieve, iterative and the semantic way of cutting chunks (vignette("segment")) need embeddings. By default harnessr asks the model provider for them, which costs a little and needs an internet connection. hr_options(embedder = "lexical") computes word-matching vectors on your machine instead. They are free, offline and exactly repeatable, but they match words and not meaning, so “turnover” will not find “revenue”. Use lexical vectors for practice and testing, and real embeddings for real work.

gr_embedders()[, c("name", "deterministic", "description")]
#>      name deterministic
#> 1     api         FALSE
#> 2 lexical          TRUE
#>                                                    description
#> 1                 Embeddings endpoint on the client's base URL
#> 2 Hashed bag-of-words; free, offline, word overlap not meaning

Reasoning effort, stage by stage

The default models reason before they answer. The provider bills that reasoning as output and counts it against the same cap as the reply, so it adds to every request’s cost. effort in gr_read_spec() sets how much reasoning to ask for: one value, such as "low", for every request, or a vector named by stage. harnessr sends it only to models it lists as reasoning models (hr_model_info(model)$reasoning). By default it sends nothing, and each request goes out at the provider’s default.

Every request a reader makes carries a label naming its stage:

reader one request per chunk the rest
stuff none stuff.answer
map_reduce map.answer reduce
refine refine.draft, then refine.revise none (the last revision is the answer); refine.answer under refine_state = "ledger"
skim skim.extract skim.consolidate (only if the passages do not fit), skim.answer
hierarchical hier.summarise.L1 hier.summarise.L2 and up, hier.answer
retrieve none retrieve.answer
rerank rerank.score (each shortlisted chunk) rerank.answer
iterative none iterative.step (one a round), iterative.final (only if no step could answer)
preview preview.skim (each skimmed section) preview.plan, preview.answer
ensemble as its members as its members, then ensemble.adjudicate

The per-chunk requests are many and each does a small job, so a lower effort saves most there; ?gr_read_spec suggests a starting profile. A name covers its own label and every label that starts with it and a dot, so map covers map.answer, and an unnamed value covers the rest.

hr_trace() records every request a run makes. Here map_reduce reads the eight chunks at low effort and merges at high:

spec <- gr_read_spec("map_reduce", model = "gpt-5.6-luna",
                     effort = c(map = "low", reduce = "high"))
tr <- hr_trace()
ans <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", hr_mock_client(stand_in), spec,
               trace = tr)
with(as.data.frame(tr), table(stage, effort))
#>             effort
#> stage        high low
#>   map.answer    0   8
#>   reduce        1   0

model = "gpt-5.6-luna" names a reasoning model. With the stand-in’s own model, harnessr would send no effort and the trace would have no effort column. A request at "high" can spend the whole output cap reasoning and come back cut off, so give it room with max_answer_tokens. gr_compare() (below) counts recipes that differ only in effort as different, so you can test what a lower effort costs. vignette("runs") covers effort across a literature review, and vignette("effort") covers effort in the core: its cost, the cache, the trace and raising it when a stage goes wrong.

Asking for citations

With cite = TRUE, the reader asks the model to cite the chunks it used, as [chunk 3]. ans$evidence leads each chunk id back to a page and section:

citing <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params)
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars [chunk 2].")
ans <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", citing,
               list(reader = "stuff", cite = TRUE))
ans$answer
#> [1] "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars [chunk 2]."
ans$evidence[ans$evidence$chunk_id == 2, c("chunk_id", "section")]
#>   chunk_id section
#> 2        2 Summary

If the model cites a chunk it was never sent, harnessr records the citation in ans$notes$cited_unknown and marks the answer partial. hierarchical does not support citations, because it answers from summaries and not from chunks.

Checking what an answer rests on

The contents of ans$evidence depend on the reader:

reader evidence$text holds
stuff, retrieve, rerank, iterative the chunks, word for word
skim passages the model copied out
map_reduce each chunk’s answer
refine, hierarchical nothing (the answer is built from drafts or summaries)

Chunks sent word for word are true copies of the document by construction. The passages skim collects are what the model says the document contains, so harnessr checks every one against the chunk it came from:

skimmed <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", hr_mock_client(stand_in), "skim")
gr_verify_evidence(skimmed)[, c("chunk_id", "verified", "match")]
#>   chunk_id verified match
#> 1        2     TRUE     1

The model below invents one. Its passage is fluent, on topic and attributed to a real chunk, yet the document does not contain it, and you could not catch it by eye:

memo <- gr_segment(gr_ingest("Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.\n\nHeadcount grew to 1,204."),
                   list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 40))
inventing <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (grepl("You extract evidence", messages[[1]]$content, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return("Revenue rose to 88.9 billion dollars on record demand.")
  }
  "Revenue was 88.9 billion dollars."
})
invented <- gr_read(memo, "What was revenue?", inventing, "skim")
gr_verify_evidence(invented)[, c("kind", "verified", "match")]
#>        kind verified match
#> 1 extracted    FALSE 0.333
invented$partial
#> [1] TRUE

match scores how much of a passage the source holds:

  • It is 1 for an exact quotation once spacing, quote marks, dashes and capitals are folded away, since a faithful quotation can differ in those. A changed figure is not folded away.
  • Below 1, it is the fraction of the passage carried by its longest consecutive run in the source. The place of a change matters as much as its size: a changed last word leaves a run of nine in ten and scores 0.9, while a changed word in the middle splits the passage and scores about 0.5.
  • Below about 0.3, no quotation is left, only shared vocabulary.

The check uses a run instead of word overlap because overlap cannot tell a quotation from a paraphrase built from the same words. A passage that does not verify gets verified = FALSE and counts in ans$notes$unverified_evidence, and any one of them makes the answer partial.

gr_read_spec(verify = TRUE) runs the same check inside gr_read(). It writes the check’s columns onto $evidence, marks the answer partial when a quotation is not found, counts the quotations it checked in notes$quotes_checked, and records a read.verify step in the trace.

It also holds iterative to quoting. Each step must list the passages its answer rests on, word for word with their chunk numbers, and the loop stops only when every one is found in the chunk it names. If a run ends with none accepted, it keeps the refused answer in notes$unverified_answer and reports the answer as not in the document.

vspec <- gr_read_spec(reader = "skim", verify = TRUE)
checked <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", hr_mock_client(stand_in), vspec)
checked$notes$quotes_checked
#> [1] 1
checked$evidence[, c("verified", "match", "quote_status", "quote_sim")]
#>   verified match quote_status quote_sim
#> 1     TRUE     1     verbatim         1

The quote_ columns come from a second matcher, which harnessr records beside verified: quote_status, quote_sim, quote_coverage, quote_edits and quote_critical_ok. It expands ligatures, joins words hyphenated across a line, and scores the closest window of the source by character edits, with numbers and negations required to be identical. Its statuses are verbatim, near_verbatim, unverified, and not_checked for a passage too long to score.

On a labelled set of 343 true and 162 false quotations, the second matcher rejects 1.2% of true ones, against 36.4% for the existing check, and accepts none with a changed digit, number word, comparison sign or negation. It does accept 25 of 46 quotations with one content word swapped as near_verbatim, so in this release it decides nothing: verified and match still decide.

The other columns of ans$evidence are page, filled in only for a PDF, section, kind, and score, which only retrieve (similarity) and rerank (the model’s 0 to 10) set. This check and the citation check above are string comparisons on text you already have, so they cost nothing and always run.

Questions that assume something false

A question can take for granted something the document contradicts: “Why did revenue fall in 2024?” asked of a report in which revenue rose. A reader then either answers on the question’s terms or says the answer is not in the document, and either way you lose what the document does say.

With premise = TRUE in gr_read_spec(), the reader tells the model to say so in one sentence when the excerpts state the opposite of something the question assumes, and to give what they state instead. That sentence is ans$answer and ans$premise, and is_not_found() is FALSE for it. Excerpts that are merely silent still count as not found.

A reader that answers in one request (stuff, retrieve, rerank, skim, hierarchical, preview) gives that request’s verdict. map_reduce passes a chunk that contradicts the question to its merge as a finding, and ans$notes$premise_chunks lists the chunks that said so, whatever the merge decided; ensemble does the same with its members (ans$notes$premise_members). ?gr_read_spec describes the rest.

The stand-in below plays a model that finds the summary contradicting the question and the other chunks silent. The reader asks the model to open such a reply with FALSE_PREMISE:, as here:

loaded <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  sent <- paste(vapply(messages[-1], function(m) m$content, character(1)),
                collapse = "\n")
  if (grepl("45.2 million", sent, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return("FALSE_PREMISE: Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars, from 38.7 million.")
  }
  "NOT_IN_DOCUMENT"
})
ans <- gr_read(chunks, "Why did revenue fall in 2024?", loaded,
               gr_read_spec("map_reduce", premise = TRUE))
ans$premise
#> [1] "Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars, from 38.7 million."
is_not_found(ans$answer)
#> [1] FALSE
ans$notes$premise_chunks
#> [1] 2

The verdict is the model’s reading of the excerpts. Under the default premise_verdict = "sentence", harnessr does not check it, so weigh it as you would any answer; "structured" (under “Premise checks” below) asks for a quotation and checks it. The check is off by default because it makes the prompts longer, so a cache or a recorded run made without it does not answer a run with it. extract and screen ignore it.

Trying readers on your own documents

To choose, test readers on a few documents whose answers you already know. gr_compare() runs several configurations on one document. It extracts the text once and shares chunks between configurations that cut them the same way:

cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue in 2024?", list(
  gr_recipe("narrow", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2)),
  gr_recipe("wide", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 6)),
  gr_recipe("all", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "map_reduce"))),
  client = hr_mock_client(stand_in))
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "reader", "settings", "chunks_used", "not_found", "partial")]
#>   recipe     reader                settings chunks_used not_found partial
#> 1 narrow   retrieve top_k=2, max_tokens=120           2     FALSE   FALSE
#> 2   wide   retrieve          max_tokens=120           6     FALSE   FALSE
#> 3    all map_reduce          max_tokens=120           8     FALSE   FALSE

settings names whatever each configuration changed from the defaults, so you can tell apart rows that differ only in a number. gr_compare() runs two configurations that would do exactly the same work once, with a warning, so you do not pay twice.

When a provider cannot do structured replies

rerank, iterative and preview ask the model to reply in a fixed structure (JSON), which most current providers support. If the provider does not support the structure or the reply cannot be read, each one falls back, warns, and marks the answer partial: rerank to word-matching order, iterative to a single retrieval, preview to reading everything. You still get an answer, and partial tells you it came by the fallback.

Every call that asks for JSON (these three, model segmentation, screening, claims, outlines and extraction) checks the reply’s types, enum values and required fields, through nested objects and arrays, before using it. harnessr treats a reply that fails as one that did not parse: the reader takes its failure path, the cache does not keep the reply, and the reason says where the reply broke the schema, as in $.groups[0]: expected array, got 1. gr_extract() still reads each field’s value itself, so “1,204” in an integer field is still 1204; the check covers only the shape of its replies.

When the answer is not what you expected

The answer object and its trace hold enough to find the cause. The table lists causes from the most common to the least:

symptom check likely cause
NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, but you can see the answer in the file nrow(ans$evidence), then gr_chunk_stats() the chunk holding it never reached the model. Lower max_tokens, raise top_k, or switch to a reader whose signature starts all\|
the answer is right but thin ans$notes$chunks against length(ans$chunks_used) most chunks answered NOT_IN_DOCUMENT. That is usually correct; if not, the chunk boundaries are cutting the evidence in half, so add overlap_tokens (vignette("segment"))
ans$partial is TRUE print(ans), then ans$notes and print(ans$trace) failed_calls (transport), dropped_chunks (did not fit), call_cap_reached or cost_cap_reached (vignette("runs")), unread_pages (no text layer and no OCR), or a merge that fell back to joining the answers
ans$notes$unverified_evidence is set gr_verify_evidence(ans) the model wrote a quotation that is not in the chunk it is attributed to. match says how far off: near 1 is a typo, near 0 is invention
ans$notes$cited_unknown is set that value against ans$chunks_used the answer cited a chunk that was never sent to it
figures, dates or percentages are missing doc$stats$clean_log a cleaning step removed them. remove_numbers is off by default; the legacy preset turns it on (vignette("ingest"))
a scanned PDF comes back nearly empty doc$stats$chars and doc$stats$unread_pages, and any gr_ocr_unavailable warning OCR did not run or is not installed. Force it with gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "always"), and check tesseract and magick are present
every chunk is the whole document nrow(doc$blocks) the file has no blank lines between paragraphs, so there is nothing to split on. Use method = "sentence" or "fixed"
the run costs far more than expected gr_readers()$cost_calls the reader makes one request per chunk and max_tokens is small. Run gr_chunk_stats() first; it is free
answers change between identical runs the temperature setting, unset by default set temperature = 0. Reasoning models ignore it (hr_model_info(m)$supports_temperature)
NOT_IN_DOCUMENT for a question that assumes something the document contradicts ans$premise, with premise = TRUE without the check a reader can only answer or say the excerpts are silent; see “Questions that assume something false” above

Test for the marker with is_not_found(ans$answer) rather than grepl("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT", ...): a real answer can quote the marker, and models decorate it (**NOT_IN_DOCUMENT.**).

Two habits keep this cheap: run gr_chunk_stats() before you spend anything, and keep hr_options(max_cost_usd = ...) set to an amount you would not mind paying by accident.

Choosing the settings

Each walkthrough below covers one reading setting or group in four parts: what it controls and trades off, the signs in your results that point to changing it, where its default came from, and how to test a change. vignette("settings") lists every reading setting with its default, and gr_settings("read") gives each one’s evidence.

The tests use hr_sweep(), which builds one arm per value of a setting, and hr_benchmark(), which runs the arms on a reference. Here they run on one question about the example report, with the stand-in model above. They show what each value sends and what hr_sweep_check() reports, and they cannot show which value answers better. vignette("compare") sweeps top_k on 16 dev questions, compares two values on 32 test questions and reads the result with intervals.

qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
reads <- hr_mock_client(stand_in)
sweep <- function(arms) {
  hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = reads, split = "dev",
               scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
}
calls <- function(bench) {
  vapply(attr(bench, "traces")[bench$ledger_id], function(t) nrow(as.data.frame(t)),
         integer(1))
}

Which reader

What it controls. The reader decides how the chunks reach the model (see “The readers” above). The main trade is between two groups:

  • Readers that send every chunk (map_reduce, refine, hierarchical, skim). Their cost grows with the document, and they cannot miss a chunk.
  • Readers that pick a few (retrieve, rerank, iterative). Their cost does not grow with the document, and they answer only from what they picked.

Within the first group, map_reduce reads each chunk alone, refine carries a draft through the document in order, hierarchical answers from summaries, and skim answers from passages it quotes, which verify can check. skim_model and summary_model put the per-chunk work of skim and hierarchical on a cheaper model.

Signs it needs changing. NOT_IN_DOCUMENT from retrieve for a fact you can find in the file, with ans$evidence holding other chunks, means the pick missed: try a reader that sends every chunk, or rerank. A bill that grows with every page added, for one-fact questions, points the other way. An answer that misses how an argument develops points to refine; one that needs exact wording to skim.

Where the default came from. gr_read_spec() defaults to map_reduce because it reads the whole document at any length. No comparison of readers is recorded (untested). answer_document() chooses "fast" or "thorough" by length (auto_max_tokens in hr_options()).

How to test it. Sweep the reader on one segmentation:

base <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                overlap_tokens = 0))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(base, list(reader = c("map_reduce", "refine", "hierarchical",
                                              "skim", "retrieve"))))
bench$calls <- calls(bench)
aggregate(cbind(calls, tokens_in) ~ param.reader, bench, mean)
#>   param.reader calls tokens_in
#> 1 hierarchical     9      1273
#> 2   map_reduce     9      1559
#> 3       refine     8      1839
#> 4     retrieve     1       584
#> 5         skim     9      1328

On eight chunks, the four readers that send every chunk make 8 or 9 requests and send 1273 to 1839 prompt tokens, while retrieve makes one request of 584. refine sends the most because every request carries the draft so far.

How many chunks: top_k and min_score

What it controls. top_k is how many chunks retrieve and rerank send, and how many iterative adds each round. More chunks make it likelier the answer is among them, and make the prompt longer and the answer’s evidence noisier. min_score drops chunks less similar to the question than a floor, keeping the best one.

Signs it needs changing. NOT_IN_DOCUMENT where ans$evidence holds chunks next to the one with the answer points to a larger top_k, and so does gr_seg_recall() finding the answer at rank 5 when top_k is 4. An answer built from several unrelated chunks, or a cost per question far above what one fact needs, points to a smaller one.

Where the default came from. The default of 6 is a common starting value for retrieval, not tuned here (untested). "needle" uses 8.

How to test it.

needle <- gr_arm("needle", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, list(top_k = c(2, 4, 8, 12))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.top_k, bench, mean)
#>   param.top_k tokens_in
#> 1           2       289
#> 2           4       449
#> 3           8       797
#> 4          12       909

The prompt grows from 289 tokens at top_k = 2 to 909 at 12. In vignette("compare") a top_k sweep on a different arm, the "fast" recipe with the retrieve reader and 40-token sentence chunks, found top_k = 2 more accurate than 4 on 32 test questions, with an interval from 1.8 to 12.0 points, and cheaper. That result holds for its arm and its stand-in model; find yours the same way.

Diversity: mmr

What it controls. Below 1, mmr trades relevance for diversity when retrieve and iterative pick chunks, so near-duplicates do not fill every place (see “Choosing and placing chunks” above). It costs no request.

Signs it needs changing. ans$evidence holding several chunks that say the same thing, from a document that repeats itself (an abstract, a summary, a conclusion), points to mmr below 1. Answers that miss the best chunk after lowering it point back up.

Where the default came from. The default of 1 is plain top-k, the selection used before the setting existed (untested). 0.7 is a common starting point for a balance.

How to test it.

bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 3, mmr = c(1, 0.7, 0.3))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                      arm              same_as runs requests      settings
#> 1 needle:top_k=3,mmr=0.7 needle:top_k=3,mmr=1    5        5 mmr: 1 vs 0.7

At 0.7 the three chunks picked were the ones plain top-k picked, so the requests were the same; only 0.3 changed them on this report. Sweep mmr only on documents that repeat themselves, and let hr_sweep_check() tell you which values sent the same requests.

Word matching: lexical_blend, bm25_k1, bm25_b and fusion

What they control. With lexical embeddings (hr_options(embedder = "lexical")), retrieve scores chunks by a blend of cosine similarity and BM25, with lexical_blend the weight on cosine. bm25_k1 sets how fast repeated words stop adding to a chunk’s score, and bm25_b how much long chunks are penalised; rerank uses BM25 to choose its candidates.

Signs they need changing. Retrieval that picks long chunks which mention the question’s words once each, over a short chunk that answers it, points to a higher bm25_b or a lower lexical_blend. With real embeddings these settings do nothing for retrieve, and hr_sweep_check() shows it.

Where the defaults came from. Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) give bm25_b = 0.75 as the usual value and bm25_k1 between 1.2 and 2.0; 1.5 lies inside that range (cited). Neither was tuned here. lexical_blend = 0.5, an even blend, was set when the offline path was written (untested).

How to test them.

bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 2, lexical_blend = c(0, 0.5, 1))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#> [1] arm      same_as  runs     requests settings
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 3, bm25_b = c(0.75, 0.3))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                         arm                    same_as runs requests
#> 1 needle:top_k=3,bm25_b=0.3 needle:top_k=3,bm25_b=0.75    5        5
#>              settings
#> 1 bm25_b: 0.75 vs 0.3

Each value of lexical_blend picked different chunks here, while bm25_b at 0.3 picked the same three as at 0.75.

fusion decides how the two rankings are combined, for retrieve and iterative alike:

  • "default" is the blend above, which retrieve applies only on lexical embeddings and iterative never did.
  • "rrf" is reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher 2009), which adds 1 / (rrf_k + rank) from each ranking, with any embeddings. It works on ranks, so one ranking’s scale cannot swamp the other’s, at the price of ignoring how far apart the scores are.

The constant rrf_k = 60 is the paper’s (cited); fusion itself is untested. Neither costs a request. A fused score lies between 0 and 2 / (rrf_k + 1), so a min_score set for cosine passes no chunk under "rrf"; retrieve then reads its best chunk alone and sets notes$below_min_score. Under mmr below 1, harnessr rescales the fused scores to 0 to 1 before weighing them against similarity.

bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 2, fusion = c("default", "rrf"),
                                            rrf_k = c(60, 5))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                                     arm                                same_as
#> 1    needle:top_k=2,fusion=rrf,rrf_k=60 needle:top_k=2,fusion=default,rrf_k=60
#> 2 needle:top_k=2,fusion=default,rrf_k=5 needle:top_k=2,fusion=default,rrf_k=60
#>   runs requests               settings
#> 1    5        5 fusion: default vs rrf
#> 2    5        5         rrf_k: 60 vs 5

On this report "rrf" with rrf_k = 60 picked the same two chunks as the blend, and rrf_k does nothing under "default", so hr_sweep_check() lists both as sending the same requests. "rrf" with rrf_k = 5 is not listed: it sent different requests. If arms differ, compare correct by param.fusion and param.rrf_k on a reference.

Placement: context_order and restate

What they control. context_order puts the chosen chunks in order of relevance, in document order, or with the best at the two ends of the prompt ("edges"). restate repeats the question before the excerpts; under "auto" that happens when they are longer than restate_tokens (1200). Both move text around and leave the choice of text alone, and restate adds the question’s length to each request.

Signs they need changing. Right answers from short prompts and misses from long ones, with the answer’s chunk sent each time, point to placement: "edges", or restate = "always". Answers that misread chunks that follow on from each other point to "document".

Where the defaults came from. "relevance" is the order the readers used before the setting existed. The alternatives were added to be compared, and no comparison is recorded. restate = "auto" was added so a comparison could measure it, and none has. restate_tokens = 1200 is an arbitrary number, kept from when it was a constant. All three are untested.

How to test them.

bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 3,
                                            context_order = c("relevance", "edges", "document"),
                                            restate = c("never", "always"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.context_order + param.restate, bench, mean)
#>   param.context_order param.restate tokens_in
#> 1            document        always       388
#> 2               edges        always       388
#> 3           relevance        always       388
#> 4            document         never       377
#> 5               edges         never       377
#> 6           relevance         never       377
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                                                    arm
#> 1  needle:top_k=3,context_order=document,restate=never
#> 2 needle:top_k=3,context_order=document,restate=always
#>                                                 same_as runs requests
#> 1  needle:top_k=3,context_order=relevance,restate=never    5        5
#> 2 needle:top_k=3,context_order=relevance,restate=always    5        5
#>                               settings
#> 1 context_order: relevance vs document
#> 2 context_order: relevance vs document

Repeating the question added 11 prompt tokens per request. "document" sent what "relevance" sent, because the three chunks chosen were already in document order; "edges" changed the requests.

Checking the answer: verify and cite

What they control. cite = TRUE asks the model to cite the chunks it used (see “Asking for citations”), which lengthens the prompt a little and lets a citation to a chunk never sent be caught. verify = TRUE checks each quotation in the answer against the chunk it names, after the reply, and marks the answer partial when one is not found (see “Checking what an answer rests on”); under iterative it also requires quotations before the loop may stop. accept_near_verbatim lets a near-verbatim quotation count there.

Signs they are needed. Answers you cannot trace to a page, or a reviewer asking where a figure came from, point to cite. Any answer you will act on without reading the source points to verify; so does a reader that quotes (skim), whose quotations are the model’s words until checked.

Where the defaults came from. Both are off, so a run sends the requests and accepts the answers it did before they existed (untested). accept_near_verbatim is off as well; on the labelled quotation set, 25 of 46 quotations with one content word swapped score near_verbatim.

How to test them.

precise <- gr_arm("precise", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                  overlap_tokens = 0))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(precise, expand.grid(cite = c(FALSE, TRUE), verify = c(FALSE, TRUE))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.cite + param.verify, bench, mean)
#>   param.cite param.verify tokens_in
#> 1      FALSE        FALSE      1328
#> 2       TRUE        FALSE      1350
#> 3      FALSE         TRUE      1328
#> 4       TRUE         TRUE      1350
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                              arm                         same_as runs requests
#> 1 precise:cite=FALSE,verify=TRUE precise:cite=FALSE,verify=FALSE    5       45
#> 2  precise:cite=TRUE,verify=TRUE  precise:cite=TRUE,verify=FALSE    5       45
#>                settings
#> 1 verify: FALSE vs TRUE
#> 2 verify: FALSE vs TRUE

cite added 22 prompt tokens to each run. verify sent the same requests as no check, because it acts on the reply. Its effect shows in which answers come back partial (ans$partial, ans$notes$unverified_evidence). Score it with a scorer that counts a partial answer as wrong, or compare the partial rate by hand.

Outcomes: answer_format

What it controls. Every answer carries ans$outcome, and is_not_found(ans) reads it. The outcome is one of "answered", "partial", "not_found", "refused" (a limit stopped the run) or "failed" (every model request the run made failed, whichever reader made it).

answer_format decides how the answering request reports the found or not-found part. "parsed" sends the free-text request and looks for NOT_IN_DOCUMENT in the reply. "schema" sends the request with a JSON schema holding answer and outcome. A reply such as “The excerpt does not mention revenue” then counts as a not-found when the model says so in outcome. A forced schema costs a few prompt tokens and needs a provider that supports structured output; published comparisons disagree on whether it changes answer quality.

Signs it needs changing. Answers that say in words that the document is silent, counted as answers because they lack the sentinel, point to "schema". Replies that fail to parse (notes$structured$parsed is FALSE) point back to "parsed" for that provider.

Where the default came from. "parsed" is what the readers sent before the setting existed (untested). The default stays until a live comparison on the default model settles the choice.

How to test it.

fields <- function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$schema_name, "answer")) {
    return('{"answer": "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", "outcome": "answered"}')
  }
  stand_in(messages, params)
}
bench <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(needle, list(answer_format = c("parsed", "schema"))), qa,
                      runs = 5, client = hr_mock_client(fields), split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(cbind(tokens_in, correct) ~ param.answer_format, bench, mean)
#>   param.answer_format tokens_in correct
#> 1              parsed       797       1
#> 2              schema       851       1

The schema’s instructions added 54 prompt tokens to each run. On a reference, compare correct, and how often answers come back not found, by param.answer_format.

Premise checks: premise and premise_verdict

What they control. premise = TRUE tells the answering requests to say when the excerpts contradict an assumption in the question (see “Questions that assume something false”). premise_verdict decides how they say it:

  • "sentence" is a FALSE_PREMISE: sentence in the reply.
  • "structured" asks, in a JSON schema, for a premise_status field and the quote from the excerpts that states the contrary. harnessr checks the quote against the excerpts that request was shown, with the matcher gr_verify_evidence() uses, and against the document where the request was shown passages or summaries a model wrote. The answer gains ans$premise_verdict.

In map_reduce, a chunk’s verdict goes to the merge only when its quote is found in that chunk; the reader drops the others and lists them in notes$premise_dropped. You pay with a longer prompt and a schema the provider must support, and get a verdict that has to point at its evidence.

Signs they need changing. Questions that take something false for granted, answered on their own terms, point to premise = TRUE. Verdicts that the document does not bear out point to "structured", which drops a map_reduce verdict with no quote behind it.

Where the defaults came from. Both are off (premise = FALSE, premise_verdict = "sentence"), so a run sends the requests it sent before (untested).

How to test them.

verdict <- function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$schema_name, "answer")) {
    return(paste0('{"answer": "Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.", ',
                  '"premise_status": "contradicted", ',
                  '"quote": "reported revenue of 45.2 million dollars"}'))
  }
  stand_in(messages, params)
}
loaded <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(fall = "Why did revenue fall in 2024?"),
                          documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                          split = "dev")
stuffed <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                   overlap_tokens = 0, reader = "stuff", premise = TRUE))
bench <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(stuffed, list(premise_verdict = c("sentence", "structured"))),
                      loaded, runs = 5, client = hr_mock_client(verdict), split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.premise_verdict, bench, mean)
#>   param.premise_verdict tokens_in
#> 1              sentence       780
#> 2            structured       844

The structured request sent 64 prompt tokens more. Score the verdicts against labels of which questions are loaded, and count how often a structured verdict’s quote verifies (ans$premise_verdict$quote_verified).

Reasoning: effort

What it controls. effort sets how much a reasoning model reasons, for every request or by stage (see “Reasoning effort, stage by stage”). The provider bills reasoning as output and counts it against the reply’s cap, so lower effort is cheaper and faster, and higher effort can help the few requests that judge or combine.

Signs it needs changing. tokens_reasoning in a benchmark, or the trace, taking most of the output of per-chunk requests points to "low" for those stages. A reply cut off (finish_reason = "length") at "high" needs a larger max_answer_tokens. Merges or final answers that miss what the per-chunk answers found point to more effort at reduce or *.answer.

Where the default came from. Unset: no effort is sent, and the provider’s own default applies (untested). ?gr_read_spec gives a starting profile, low for the many mechanical requests and high for the few that judge, which is not a measured default.

How to test it. Effort is sent only to a model harnessr lists as a reasoning model, so the arms name one. A map goes in a list column:

luna <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                overlap_tokens = 0, model = "gpt-5.6-luna"))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(luna, data.frame(effort = I(list(
  "low", c(map = "low", reduce = "high"), "high")))))
unique(bench$arm)
#> [1] "thorough:effort=low"                                
#> [2] "thorough:effort=c(map = \"low\", reduce = \"high\")"
#> [3] "thorough:effort=high"

Compare usd, tokens_reasoning and correct by param.effort on your own reference. The stand-in model reports no reasoning tokens, so here only the requests differ.

Merges: max_merge_levels

What it controls. If the findings of map_reduce, skim and the other merging readers do not fit one merge request, the reader merges them in levels. max_merge_levels caps the levels. Past the cap, the reader returns its findings unmerged and cut, and marks the answer partial. fan_in and max_levels play the same parts for hierarchical’s summaries.

Signs it needs changing. A partial answer whose notes say a merge fell back to joining the answers, on a very long document, points to a higher cap (or to larger chunks, which make fewer findings). A cost dominated by reduce requests points to a lower one.

Where the default came from. 6, the cap the merge code had as a constant; not tuned (untested).

How to test it.

bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(base, list(max_merge_levels = c(1, 6))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                           arm                     same_as runs requests
#> 1 thorough:max_merge_levels=6 thorough:max_merge_levels=1    5       45
#>                   settings
#> 1 max_merge_levels: 1 vs 6

Eight findings merge in one level, so a cap of 1 sent the same requests as 6 on this report. Test the cap on your longest documents, where it can bind.

What a request keeps: context_policy and refine_state

What they control. If the text a request carries does not fit, a reader cuts it, and every reader keeps the start of what it cuts. context_policy, an hr_context_policy(), states once what to do instead:

  • which pieces are never cut (pin);
  • which are cut first (cut_order);
  • which part of a cut piece is kept (keep: "head", "tail" or "both" ends).

The readers have no scores for their pieces, so they read a "scored" rule as "head"; hr_truncate() and hr_context_fit() take scores directly. The policy applies to refine’s draft and excerpt, the findings a merge combines, hierarchical’s summaries and preview’s outline and skims. The readers that pack whole chunks write a "truncate" step naming the chunks they left out. With order_merges = TRUE, merges and the ensemble adjudication place their findings by context_order.

refine_state decides what refine carries down the document. Under "draft", it carries a draft it rewrites with each chunk. Under "ledger", it carries a numbered ledger of findings that each request adds to, replaces or drops from, with one more request at the end to answer from it. A rewritten draft can lose a finding no later chunk restores. A ledger keeps every finding no edit names, word for word, and costs one more request.

Signs they need changing. "truncate" steps in the trace (where, tokens_dropped) on the requests whose answers are wrong show that a cut lost what was needed, and dropped_part names the part that went. A fact stated early in a long document and missing from refine’s answer, or a figure that a later correction should have replaced, points to refine_state = "ledger". gr_condensation_check() (see vignette("evaluate")) builds a test of exactly that.

Where the defaults came from. context_policy = NULL keeps the cuts every reader made before the setting existed, and refine_state = "draft" keeps the state refine carried. Nobody has compared either with the alternatives (untested).

How to test them.

ledger_reads <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (grepl("Reply with the edits", messages[[length(messages)]]$content, fixed = TRUE)) {
    excerpt <- messages[[4]]$content
    if (grepl("revenue of [0-9.]+ million", excerpt)) {
      return("ADD: Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
    }
    return("NONE")
  }
  stand_in(messages, params)
})
arms <- hr_sweep(base, list(reader = "refine", refine_state = c("draft", "ledger")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = ledger_reads, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
bench$calls <- calls(bench)
aggregate(cbind(calls, tokens_in, correct) ~ param.refine_state, bench, mean)
#>   param.refine_state calls tokens_in correct
#> 1              draft     8      1839       1
#> 2             ledger     9      2251       1

The ledger made 9 requests to the draft’s 8, the last one answering from the list, and sent 2251 prompt tokens to 1839 because its instructions are longer. Both answered right. To try a policy, give one arm an hr_context_policy() and compare the "truncate" steps of the two:

tight <- function(policy) {
  gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120, overlap_tokens = 0,
                          reader = "refine", context_policy = policy))
}
arms <- hr_sweep(function(keep) {
  tight(if (keep != "none") hr_context_policy(keep = keep))
}, list(keep = c("none", "tail")))
length(arms)
#> [1] 2

The example report fits every request whole, so nothing is cut here. On your own long documents, run the arms with hr_benchmark() as above.

Preview safeguards: unskip_k and reread_on

What they control. preview follows a plan its first request makes. By default it does not read a section the plan skips. Two settings guard against a bad plan:

  • unskip_k reads the k sections that match the question’s words best (BM25 over each section’s text) even when the plan skips them, so a plan cannot drop the one section that holds the question’s words. It costs no request, but the answer prompt grows by the sections it adds.
  • reread_on = "not_found" follows an answer of NOT_IN_DOCUMENT with one more request over the sections not read in full, trading at most one request for a second look.

Whatever the settings, the trace records every skip as a preview.skip step with its score.

Signs they need changing. NOT_IN_DOCUMENT from preview for a fact you can find, where ans$notes$plan shows its section skipped, or a preview.skip step in the trace with a high score, points to unskip_k = 1. Not-found answers on questions you know the document answers point to reread_on = "not_found".

Where the defaults came from. Both are off (unskip_k = 0, reread_on = "never"), so preview makes the requests it made before they existed (untested).

How to test them. In this test, the plan skips the summary, which holds the revenue figure:

skips_summary <- function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$schema_name, "reading_plan")) {
    return(paste0('{"sections": [{"id": 1, "treatment": "read", "reason": "Title."}, ',
                  '{"id": 2, "treatment": "skip", "reason": "A summary repeats."}]}'))
  }
  stand_in(messages, params)
}
looks <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                 overlap_tokens = 0, reader = "preview"))
bench <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(looks, expand.grid(unskip_k = c(0, 1),
                                                  reread_on = c("never", "not_found"))),
                      qa, runs = 5, client = hr_mock_client(skips_summary), split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.unskip_k + param.reread_on, bench, mean)
#>   param.unskip_k param.reread_on tokens_in
#> 1              0           never      1537
#> 2              1           never      1643
#> 3              0       not_found      1537
#> 4              1       not_found      1643
hr_sweep_check(bench)
#>                                       arm                             same_as
#> 1 thorough:unskip_k=0,reread_on=not_found thorough:unskip_k=0,reread_on=never
#> 2 thorough:unskip_k=1,reread_on=not_found thorough:unskip_k=1,reread_on=never
#>   runs requests                      settings
#> 1    5       10 reread_on: never vs not_found
#> 2    5       10 reread_on: never vs not_found

unskip_k = 1 put the summary back into the answer prompt, 106 prompt tokens more. reread_on sent nothing more here because the stand-in model never answers NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, and hr_sweep_check() lists those arms as sending the same requests as the arms without it. Test it on questions your reader misses.

Low rerank scores: low_score

What it controls. rerank drops every candidate the model scores below rerank_min_score (4 of 10). If that drops all of them, the default (low_score = "not_found") makes no answer request and returns NOT_IN_DOCUMENT with notes$retrieval_low_score = TRUE. "read_top_k" sends the 5 best-scored candidates to the answer request anyway: one request more on those questions, in exchange for not trusting the scorer’s pessimism. A not-found from that request carries retrieval_low_score too, and any answer from it carries read_below_min_score.

Signs it needs changing. NOT_IN_DOCUMENT with retrieval_low_score on questions the document answers, where the trace’s rerank.score replies rate the right chunk low, points to "read_top_k" or a lower rerank_min_score. Answers from chunks that do not hold them, after switching, point back.

Where the default came from. "not_found" is what rerank did before the setting existed (untested). rerank_min_score = 4 was set when the reader was written and not tuned.

How to test it. In this test, a cut of 10 rejects every candidate:

ranks <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                 overlap_tokens = 0, reader = "rerank",
                                 rerank_min_score = 10))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(ranks, list(low_score = c("not_found", "read_top_k"))))
bench$calls <- calls(bench)
aggregate(cbind(calls, correct) ~ param.low_score, bench, mean)
#>   param.low_score calls correct
#> 1       not_found     8       0
#> 2      read_top_k     9       1

At the default the run ends after the scoring requests and is wrong; "read_top_k" makes the answer request and gets the figure.

Composing a run from steps

gr_step() builds one stage of a run (ingest, segment or read) as a step, a function of (input, ctx). gr_step_retrieve() ranks the chunks and keeps the best, as retrieve does, without asking for an answer. Both check a step’s settings when they build it. Inside an hr_arm(), the steps use the run’s client and trace, so a benchmark counts and limits their requests:

steps <- list(gr_step("segment", method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                      overlap_tokens = 0),
              gr_step_retrieve(top_k = 2),
              gr_step("read", reader = "stuff"))
steps[[2]]
#> <gr_step> retrieve (retrieve): top_k=2
by_hand <- hr_arm("rank-then-stuff",
                  function(item, ctx) Reduce(function(x, step) step(x, ctx), steps, item))
bench <- sweep(list(by_hand, needle))
aggregate(cbind(tokens_in, correct) ~ arm, bench, mean)
#>               arm tokens_in correct
#> 1          needle       797       1
#> 2 rank-then-stuff       267       1

The hand-built arm ranks with retrieve’s ranking and then reads the two chunks it kept with stuff, so it sent 267 prompt tokens to the "needle" recipe’s 797. ?gr_step says what passes between the steps. hr_chain() runs steps like these in order as one arm and checks their order, and vignette("compose") covers it.
